name: Question 4
worked_solution:
We use the identity $\operatorname{tan}⁡2x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\operatorname{tan}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=2x.$ Then $\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.$ 

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=2x.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{6}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{3}$ |

Therefore, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡u}{2}{|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{2}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let u=2x. Then dx=12du.

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule u=2x.

x 0 π6

Therefore, the integral in terms of the new variable is ∫0π/6sin⁡(2x)dx=∫0π/3sin⁡u⋅12du=12∫0π/3sin⁡udu=−cos⁡u2|0π/3=−12(cos⁡(π3)−cos⁡(0))=−12⋅(12−1)=14.
